result: Elp1 protein is enriched in the cytoplasm of differentiated trigeminal ganglion neurons, including both neural crest- and placode-derived neurons, with highest expression in axons. At E10.5, Elp1 is initially expressed in placode-derived neurons, while condensed neural crest cells express little to no Elp1. By E11.5, Elp1 is observed in all differentiated neurons irrespective of developmental origin.
evaluation: Claims C42-C48 provide immunohistochemistry data from multiple developmental timepoints (E10.5-E12.5) showing Elp1 protein localization in differentiated neurons (identified by Islet1, β-tubulin III) but not in undifferentiated neural crest cells (identified by Neuropilin 2, Pax3, Sox10). The temporal progression and cell-type specificity are well-documented with appropriate markers and imaging data (Figure 1).

result: Elp1 is not required for initial trigeminal ganglion formation at E10.5. Control and Elp1 CKO embryos show similar trigeminal ganglion size, nerve branch presence, nerve lengths, and ratios of placodal neurons to neural crest cells.
evaluation: Claims C49-C55 provide quantitative measurements (ganglion size, nerve lengths) and immunohistochemistry data showing no significant differences between Control and Elp1 CKO at E10.5. Statistical tests (unpaired t-tests with multiple comparison adjustments) support the lack of differences. The placode-derived geniculate ganglion also shows no changes, serving as an appropriate control (C55).

result: By E11.5, Elp1 CKO trigeminal neurons exhibit abnormal axon outgrowth with disorganized, defasciculated axons in the maxillary and mandibular nerves, while the placode-derived chorda tympani nerve remains normal. Trigeminal ganglion size and cellular composition remain unchanged at this stage.
evaluation: Claims C57-C65 provide whole-mount immunohistochemistry images and quantitative data showing axon disorganization in Elp1 CKO at E11.5 (Figure 3). The phenotype is described as highly penetrant across all examined embryos (C61). The normal appearance of the placode-derived chorda tympani nerve (C62) serves as an internal control, supporting the neural crest-specific effect.

result: By E12.5, trigeminal ganglion and nerve morphology are drastically altered in Elp1 CKO with context-dependent defects in different nerve branches. The central nerve root diameter is significantly reduced, frontal nerve branching complexity is decreased, nasal nerves are absent, and infraorbital nerve extent is reduced.
evaluation: Claims C66-C73 provide detailed morphological analysis with quantitative measurements (modified Sholl analysis for branching complexity, nerve extent measurements) and whole-mount imaging (Figure 4). Statistical significance is demonstrated for central root diameter (C68) and infraorbital nerve extent (C73). The observation of distinct phenotypes in different nerve branches (C74) is well-supported by the diverse defects documented.

result: TrkA expression and TrkA-expressing neurons are specifically reduced in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia and nerves at E12.5-E13, while TrkB and TrkC expression and neuron numbers remain unchanged. TrkA neurons are reduced by 23% in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls.
evaluation: Claims C75-C82 provide both whole-mount and section immunohistochemistry data with quantitative measurements of TrkA, TrkB, and TrkC immunofluorescence and neuron counts (Figure 5). Statistical analysis shows significant reduction in TrkA (p=0.0037 for fluorescence, 23% reduction in neuron number) but no changes in TrkB or TrkC. The specificity of the TrkA defect is well-documented across multiple assays.

result: Most TrkA neurons in Elp1 CKO at E12.5 are devoid of Elp1 protein, while the majority of remaining Elp1-positive neurons express TrkB or TrkC.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization of Elp1 with different Trk receptors in Control and Elp1 CKO (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). This provides direct evidence that the neural crest-specific deletion of Elp1 primarily affects TrkA neurons, consistent with the lineage data.

result: TrkB and TrkC neurons are born first in the trigeminal ganglion followed by TrkA neurons. Six1 expression shifts from predominantly TrkB/TrkC neurons at E10.5 to predominantly TrkA neurons at E11.5-E12.5, suggesting Six1 is a marker of recently differentiated neurons rather than an exclusive marker of placodal lineage.
evaluation: Claims C86-C94 provide detailed temporal analysis of Trk receptor expression and Six1 co-localization across multiple developmental stages (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Quantitative data show the shift in Six1 expression from TrkB/TrkC neurons (78-92% at E10.5) to TrkA neurons (86% at E11.5, 51% at E12.5). The interpretation that Six1 marks recently differentiated neurons (C95) is a reasonable inference from the temporal correlation with neurogenesis timing.

result: Lineage tracing using Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice shows that at E10.5, 92.1% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells express GFP, while only 12.1% of Six1-positive cells are GFP-positive, confirming most Six1-positive cells are placode-derived at this stage. By E12.5, 91.7% of Six1-positive cells express GFP, indicating a shift to mostly neural crest-derived Six1-expressing cells.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 provide quantitative lineage tracing data with clear percentages and appropriate controls (Figure 7). The high efficiency of Wnt1-Cre recombination in Sox10-positive cells (92.1%) validates the approach. The temporal shift in Six1-positive cell lineage from predominantly placode (87.9% at E10.5) to predominantly neural crest (91.7% at E12.5) is well-documented.

result: At E15.5, approximately three quarters of TrkA neurons are neural crest-derived (75.6% GFP-positive), while approximately three quarters of TrkB and TrkC neurons are placode-derived (77.4% and 78.6% RFP-positive, respectively). This demonstrates a strong correlation between cellular origin and Trk receptor expression.
evaluation: Claims C101-C104 provide quantitative lineage tracing data at E15.5 using the Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG reporter (Figure 8). The percentages are clearly stated and the inverse relationship between TrkA (mostly neural crest) and TrkB/TrkC (mostly placode) is well-documented. The inference of correlation between lineage and Trk expression (C105) is well-supported by the data.

result: Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia show significantly increased TUNEL staining at E12.5, with TUNEL-positive nuclei often found in TrkA-expressing cells. NGF expression in target tissues is unchanged. The placode-derived geniculate ganglion shows no increased apoptosis, suggesting neural crest-derived neurons are most affected.
evaluation: Claims C106-C107 provide quantitative TUNEL data showing statistically significant increase in Elp1 CKO (p=0.0052) with co-localization to TrkA neurons (Figure 9). The observation that NGF expression is unchanged (C110, Figure 9—figure supplement 2) rules out one potential mechanism. The lack of increased apoptosis in the placode-derived geniculate ganglion (C111) serves as an appropriate control supporting the neural crest-specific effect (C112).

result: Elp1 protein expression is more selectively expressed in neurons compared to β-galactosidase in Elp1LacZ mice, suggesting potential post-transcriptional or post-translational regulation. The enrichment of Elp1 in neuronal cytoplasm and axons suggests extranuclear functions.
evaluation: Claims C114-C115 present a speculative interpretation of the difference between Elp1 protein and β-galactosidase expression patterns. While the observation is valid (C114), the proposed mechanism (C115) is explicitly speculative and alternative explanations (different protein half-lives, detection threshold differences) are mentioned but not tested. Claim C116 makes a reasonable inference about extranuclear functions based on subcellular localization, supported by citations to similar findings in other systems.

result: Elp1 is not required for trunk neural crest cell migration or formation of dorsal root or sympathetic ganglia, though other elongator subunits like Elp3 may have distinct functions in neural crest migration.
evaluation: Claim C117 is supported by citations to multiple previous studies and is consistent with the current observation that trigeminal ganglion formation appears normal at E10.5. Claims C118-C119 cite a previous study showing different effects of Elp3 knockdown, supporting the interpretation that elongator subunits may have distinct functions. However, this result is primarily based on prior work rather than new data from this manuscript.

result: Different trigeminal nerve branches show distinct phenotypes in Elp1 CKO: frontal nerve axons reach targets but retract, while nasal nerve axons fail to navigate to targets. This suggests context-dependent mechanisms and that Elp1 is required for axonal outgrowth and proper target innervation.
evaluation: Claims C120-C121 make reasonable inferences from the temporal imaging data showing frontal nerve branches present at E12.5 but reduced by E13 (retraction), versus nasal nerves that never form (navigation failure). The interpretation that Elp1 is required for axonal outgrowth and innervation (C122) and that multiple context-dependent mechanisms are involved (C123) are well-supported by the diverse phenotypes documented across different nerve branches.

result: Loss of Elp1 from neural crest cells has major effects after neuronal differentiation rather than during neurogenesis. Unlike in dorsal root ganglia where Elp1 loss affects Pax3-positive progenitors, trigeminal ganglion Pax3-positive cells express little Elp1 and are glial rather than neuronal progenitors.
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 provide data and citations distinguishing the trigeminal ganglion from dorsal root ganglia. The observation of normal Six1-positive neuron numbers at E11.5 (C125) and low Elp1 expression in Pax3-positive cells (C126) support the interpretation that neurogenesis is not primarily affected (C128). The conclusion that Elp1 effects occur after differentiation (C129) is a reasonable inference from the temporal data, though the authors acknowledge not definitively ruling out neurogenic deficits.

result: While Elp1 has been reported to modulate TrkA/NGF retrograde signaling in sympathetic neurons, several observations in the trigeminal ganglion (loss of TrkA in distal axons, absence of some nerve branches, normal NGF expression) suggest additional or alternative mechanisms beyond retrograde signaling deficits.
evaluation: Claims C130-C131 cite previous work on TrkA signaling. Claims C132-C134 present observations from the current study that are inconsistent with a simple retrograde signaling deficit model: reduced TrkA expression in axon terminals (C133), complete absence of some nerves (C134), and normal NGF in targets (C132). The authors appropriately note these contradictions and suggest the need for additional mechanisms, making this a well-reasoned critical analysis of their data.

result: Elp1 may function in axonal outgrowth through NGF-independent mechanisms including anterograde trafficking, local protein synthesis, axon guidance, or inter-axonal adhesion. Supporting evidence includes reduced Cadherin-7 in Elp1 CKO dorsal root ganglia and broad proteomic changes affecting axon guidance pathways.
evaluation: Claims C136, C139, and C140 are explicitly speculative, proposing potential mechanisms without direct testing. Claims C137-C138 and C141-C143 cite previous studies showing gene expression changes, proteomic alterations, and Cadherin-7 reduction in other systems, but these are not directly demonstrated in the trigeminal ganglion in this study. While these are reasonable hypotheses for future investigation, they remain speculative in the context of the current work.

result: The mouse trigeminal ganglion is a mosaic of neural crest- and placode-derived neurons with no spatial segregation by lineage, unlike the chick. The Trk-expressing neuronal composition is established during mid- to late-gestation and remains constant into early postnatal life.
evaluation: Claims C144-C148 cite previous literature establishing differences between chick and mouse trigeminal ganglion organization and the correlation between cell size and lineage. Claim C149 cites a recent study showing similar proportions of Wnt1-Cre-recombined TrkA neurons in postnatal mice. Claim C150 makes a reasonable inference from comparing the current embryonic data with the cited postnatal data, though direct longitudinal tracking was not performed.

result: The 22q11DS deletion mouse shows targeted effects on TrkA neurons preceded by premature neurogenic divisions of neural crest cells and increased variation of neuronal gene expression at E9.5 and E10.5.
evaluation: Claim C151 cites findings from a recent study (Karpinski et al., 2022) and is used to provide context for the current findings. This is appropriately cited prior work rather than a new result from this manuscript.

result: Placode-derived TrkB and TrkC neurons show no defects in Elp1 CKO at examined stages, and the placode-derived geniculate ganglion shows no perturbations. A placode-targeted deletion of Elp1 would likely affect TrkB neurons based on expression patterns and studies in epibranchial ganglia.
evaluation: Claims C152-C153 state observations from the current study showing no effects on placode-derived neurons in the neural crest-specific knockout. Claim C154 cites a recent study on epibranchial ganglia. Claims C155-C156 are speculative predictions about what would happen with a placode-specific deletion, appropriately framed as speculation and based on reasonable extrapolation from Elp1 expression patterns and cited studies.

result: Innervation of the whisker pad is initiated by E11.5 in both Control and Elp1 CKO, but the innervation field does not expand substantially in Elp1 CKO. Early maxillary nerve fibers at E11 express predominantly TrkB or TrkC, suggesting placode-derived neurons may reach targets first and act as scaffolds for later TrkA axons.
evaluation: Claims C157-C158 are supported by whole-mount imaging data (Figures 3-5). Claim C160 provides immunohistochemistry data showing the predominance of TrkB/TrkC in early maxillary nerve fibers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Claim C159 is a speculative interpretation but is reasonable given the temporal sequence of TrkB/TrkC versus TrkA neurogenesis and the observation that some innervation occurs in Elp1 CKO despite TrkA deficits.

result: The Wnt1-Cre driver targets approximately 90% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells in the trigeminal ganglion, similar to previous reports in the trunk. While a population of non-recombined neural crest derivatives remains, Wnt1-Cre is commonly used and achieves more efficient recombination than other drivers like Sox10-Cre.
evaluation: Claim C162 provides quantitative data (92.1% recombination efficiency) supported by Figure 7 and cited comparison to trunk studies. Claims C161 and C163 acknowledge the limitation of incomplete recombination. Claims C164-C165 cite previous literature justifying the use of Wnt1-Cre despite this limitation. This is an appropriate discussion of experimental limitations and validation of the approach.

result: Elp1 CKO phenotypes are more extreme than human FD due to complete loss of Elp1 from neural crest derivatives, whereas FD patients retain some Elp1 protein. It is unclear whether certain neuronal subpopulations are more affected in FD patients.
evaluation: Claims C166-C167 appropriately compare the mouse model to human disease, citing the molecular basis of FD (Slaugenhaupt et al., 2001). Claim C168 acknowledges a knowledge gap in understanding cellular-level effects in human patients. This is an appropriate discussion of model limitations and translational considerations.
